facts.statement: Echinochimaera is considered one of the earliest known chimaeriform fish.
facts.quote: It is one of the earliest Chimaeriformes known.

facts.statement: The genus name Echinochimaera combines the Greek word for 'spiny' with 'chimaera'.
facts.quote: The genus' name derives from the Greek εχινό (echino) meaning spiny, and chimaera.

facts.statement: Echinochimaera is classified within the order Chimaeriformes.
facts.quote: It is assigned to the order Chimaeriformes.

facts.statement: The two known species of Echinochimaera lived during the Upper Mississippian (Serpukhovian) stage.
facts.quote: The two known Echinochimaera species lived in the Upper Mississippian (Serpukhovian).

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that the paddle-like tails indicate E. meltoni was likely neither a predator nor a fast swimmer.
facts.quote: The paddle-like tails indicate that E. meltoni was likely not a predator nor a fast swimmer.

facts.statement: E. meltoni was first described by Richard Lund in 1977.
facts.quote: E. meltoni was first described by Richard Lund, an Adelphi University palaeontologist, in 1977.

facts.statement: Fossils of E. meltoni show extreme sexual dimorphism, with males reaching a maximum length of 15 cm and females only 7 cm.
facts.quote: The fossils found of E. meltoni have shown a great deal of sexual dimorphism, with males being found to have a maximum body length of 15 cm while that found in females was only 7 cm.

facts.statement: Males of E. meltoni had four pairs of spikes that may have served for defense and sexual identification.
facts.quote: Males also had four pairs of spikes which may have been used to defend against predators and to identify the fish as male.

facts.statement: The abundance of immature male fossils combined with significant sexual dimorphism indicates extreme sexual selection in E. meltoni.
facts.quote: There was a relative abundance of immature male fossils found, and that together with the significant sexual dimorphism indicate there was extreme sexual selection among the species.

facts.statement: E. snyderi was also described by Richard Lund.
facts.quote: E. snyderi was described, like E. meltoni, by Richard Lund.

facts.statement: Later discoveries of mature specimens suggest E. snyderi reached a larger adult size than E. meltoni.
facts.quote: Mature specimens discovered later suggest this species' adult size to be larger than E. meltoni.

facts.statement: Echinochimaera was an extinct genus of holosteans living in the Lower Carboniferous, approximately 355 million years ago.
facts.quote: Echinochimaera es un género extinto de holocéfalos del orden Chimaeriformes que vivió en el Carbonífero Inferior, hace unos 355 millones de años.

facts.statement: Echinochimaera reached a maximum length of less than 30 cm.
facts.quote: Llegaba a medir menos de 30 cm de largo.

facts.statement: Echinochimaera had a rounded body, large pectoral fins, and two dorsal fins, one of which possessed a movable spine.
facts.quote: Tenía un cuerpo redondeado, grandes aletas pectorales y dos aletas dorsales, dotada una de ellas una espina móvil.

facts.statement: The body shape, fins, and paddle-like tail indicate that Echinochimaera was a slow swimmer and likely not a predator.
facts.quote: La forma de su cuerpo y sus aletas, así como la cola en forma de paleta, indican que este animal era un nadador lento, y probablemente no era un depredador.

facts.statement: Echinochimaera is assigned to the family Echinochimaeridae.
The time range for Echinochimaera is the Serpukhovian, from 326.9 to 323.6 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Serpukhovian to Serpukhovian (326.9 to 323.6 million years ago)
